title: Art History · Episode 1
chapters: Michelangelo and the Sistine Chapel ceiling

units.t: Art History. Episode one.
In this episode: The first artists, The colourful history of paint, Aboriginal art and Michelangelo and the Sistine Chapel ceiling.
Part one. The first artists.
Tens of thousands of years before writing, people crawled into dark caves and painted animals so well they still take your breath away.
Older than writing.
Writing is only about 5,000 years old, but people made pictures long before that.
Painted and engraved animals, people and hands have been found on every inhabited continent.
For a long time Europe was thought to be the birthplace of cave art.

Discoveries on Sulawesi, Indonesia, overturned that: hand stencils were dated in 2014 to about 40,000 years, a warty pig painting at least 45,500 years in 2021, and a scene of human-like figures with a pig at least 51,200 years in 2024.
These dates come from mineral crusts that formed over the paint, so they are minimum ages.
A hand stencil on the Indonesian island of Muna, dated in 2026, is at least 67,800 years old, the oldest known rock art.
Art is one of the oldest things our species does.
Lascaux and Chauvet.
In September 1940, four teenagers followed a hole near Montignac, France, and found Lascaux, with around 600 paintings and 1,500 engravings made roughly 17,000 years ago.
Its Hall of the Bulls shows horses, deer and huge aurochs, an extinct wild cattle.
Visitors' breath and body heat damaged the walls, so the cave closed to the public in 1963.
Today people visit replicas.
In 1994, three explorers found Chauvet Cave in the Ardèche.
Its paintings are more than 30,000 years old, roughly twice Lascaux's age, yet just as skilful.
The artists used shading, scraped the rock paler, and drew overlapping outlines that suggest movement, like frames of animation.
Many animals are dangerous ones: cave lions, woolly rhinoceroses, mammoths and bears.
Chauvet has never been opened to the public; a replica opened nearby in 2015.
Australia's living art.
Australia has one of the largest and longest rock art traditions in the world, created by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples.
In the Kimberley, Gwion Gwion paintings show elegant figures with tassels and headdresses, and a painted kangaroo is about 17,000 years old.
Arnhem Land and Kakadu sites such as Ubirr show fish and animals in 'x-ray' style.
Murujuga on the Burrup Peninsula holds more than a million engravings, and joined the World Heritage List in 2025.
European cave art's meaning is guesswork, but much Australian rock art is different.
Traditional Owners still care for the sites and know the stories, and in places have repainted them within living memory.
Some Arnhem Land paintings even show Macassan boats and European ships.
Many sites are sacred.
Go with a guide or follow posted guidance, and never touch the paintings.
Why make it.
For the ancient European caves, we can only infer purpose, and every theory is debated.
Early scholars suggested 'hunting magic', painting animals to help catch them, but the animals shown often don't match what people mostly ate.
Others argue the deep, hard-to-reach chambers point to ritual or spiritual experience.
Art may also have passed on knowledge about animals and seasons, told stories, or marked who belonged to a place.
Handprints feel like a signature: 'I was here.'
It is likely there was no single reason, just as there isn't for art today.
What this means.
Cave art is a reminder that people tens of thousands of years ago were not simple or primitive.
They had the same brains we do, and the same urge to observe carefully, remember and share.
When you look at a Chauvet lion or a Kimberley figure, you are seeing the work of someone who studied the world closely and wanted it to last.
You can explore online virtual tours of Lascaux and Chauvet, visit rock art sites in Kakadu or near Sydney with a guide, and read about the Traditional Owners who care for them.
The key idea: Art is far older than writing, and some of the oldest known images come from Indonesia, not Europe.
Part two. The colourful history of paint.
Some colours were once worth more than gold.
Others were made from snails, insects or even Egyptian mummies.
The story of pigments is a story of trade, chemistry, danger and luck.
Earth in your palm.
Pick up a lump of red or yellow earth, grind it to powder, mix it with water or fat, and you have paint.
Ochre, a clay coloured by iron oxides, is among the oldest pigments people used.
Humans were collecting and processing it tens of thousands of years ago, and it appears in ancient rock art worldwide.
In Australia, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have used ochre for a very long time, for painting rock, bark and bodies, and in ceremony.
Some sources were highly valued and traded over long distances.
Heating yellow ochre turns it red, a trick early people seem to have discovered.
Earth colours such as raw sienna and burnt umber remain on every artist's palette today.
Colours worth more than gold.
The finest medieval and Renaissance blue came from the mines of Badakhshan in what is now Afghanistan, where lapis lazuli was dug from the mountains.
Grinding the stone gave a dull greyish powder, so craftspeople kneaded it in a dough of wax and resin and washed out the pure blue particles.
The result, ultramarine, meaning 'from beyond the sea', could cost more than gold by weight.
Contracts sometimes specified how much a painter had to use, and it was often kept for the robes of the Virgin Mary.
The city of Tyre, in today's Lebanon, became famous for a dye from murex sea snails.
Each snail yields a tiny amount, so the dye needed vast numbers and smelled awful.
In ancient Rome, a purple stripe marked senators, and emperors claimed the deepest purple for themselves.
Beautiful and deadly.
Many old pigments were dangerous.
Lead white, the main white paint for centuries, was toxic, and painters who handled it often risked lead poisoning.
In 1775 the Swedish chemist Carl Wilhelm Scheele made a vivid green from copper and arsenic.
Scheele's green, and the related emerald green, became fashionable in the nineteenth century for wallpapers, clothing and even sweets.
They released arsenic as they aged or got damp, harming the people who lived with them.
Then there was mummy brown, a rich paint made from ground-up Egyptian mummies and sold by colourmakers until the twentieth century.
Some artists were horrified when they learned what it contained.
Modern artists' paints are far safer, and labels warn about the few hazardous pigments still sold.
Accidents and the paint tube.
Around 1706 in Berlin, a colourmaker trying to make red ended up with deep blue, apparently because an ingredient was contaminated.
Prussian blue, cheaper than ultramarine, became one of the first modern synthetic pigments, used in painting, printing and engineers' blueprints.
In 1856 eighteen-year-old William Henry Perkin, a London chemistry student, tried to make the malaria drug quinine from coal tar.
He failed, but noticed a purple residue that dyed silk beautifully.
He called it mauveine and started a business.
Mauve became a craze and helped launch the synthetic dye industry.
In 1841 John Goffe Rand, an American portrait painter in London, patented a collapsible metal paint tube with a screw cap.
Paint became portable, making it easier to paint outdoors, as the French Impressionists often did.
Colours still being invented.
The search for new colours has not ended.
In 2009 a team led by chemist Mas Subramanian at Oregon State University was experimenting with materials for electronics when a sample came out of the furnace a brilliant blue.
Named YInMn blue after yttrium, indium and manganese, it was the first new inorganic blue pigment in about two centuries, and it is very stable.
In 2014 a British company announced Vantablack, a coating of tiny carbon tubes that absorbs almost all visible light, making objects look like holes in space.
When the sculptor Anish Kapoor obtained exclusive rights to use it in art, other artists protested.
The artist Stuart Semple responded by releasing his own pink paint that anyone could buy except Kapoor.
The key idea: Ochre, a clay coloured by iron oxides, is one of humanity's oldest pigments and is still used today.
Part three. Aboriginal art.
The world's oldest continuous art tradition is also one of its most exciting contemporary art movements, and it has never been just one style.
Not one style.
At the time of British colonisation, Australia was home to more than 250 distinct Aboriginal languages, each belonging to its own peoples with their own Country, law and stories.
Art reflects that diversity.
Dot painting from the Central and Western Desert is famous, but it is only one tradition.
Arnhem Land is known for bark painting and fine cross-hatching called rarrk.
The Tiwi Islands have bold ochre designs and carved poles.
South-eastern peoples carved trees and made possum-skin cloaks.
Torres Strait Islanders, a distinct culture, are renowned for masks, headdresses and linocut prints.
Art as law and story.
In many Aboriginal cultures, art is not separate from law, religion and knowledge of the land.
Designs can record ancestral beings and their journeys, show waterholes and landmarks, or identify the family groups responsible for a place.
'Dreaming' is the English word often used for this body of law and story, though each language has its own term, such as Tjukurrpa in parts of the Western Desert.
Many prefer it to 'Dreamtime' because it is ongoing.
Desert paintings often share a visual language: concentric circles can mean a waterhole or campsite, U shapes people seated, and lines travel.
Early Papunya paintings showed some sacred designs openly, which caused distress.
Artists responded partly with dots and infill, sharing a story publicly while keeping its deepest meanings for those entitled to know.
Bark and Papunya.
Rock art across Australia stretches back tens of thousands of years.
Bark painting, done with natural ochres on flattened stringybark, is strongly associated with Arnhem Land, and it became politically powerful.
In 1963, Yolŋu people at Yirrkala sent federal parliament petitions typed on paper and framed by bark paintings, protesting a bauxite mine on their land.
They are foundational documents of the land rights movement and are still displayed at Parliament House in Canberra.
In 1971 at Papunya, west of Alice Springs, teacher Geoffrey Bardon encouraged senior men to paint a mural on the school wall.
Men began painting ancestral designs, once made in sand or on the body, in acrylic on board and later canvas.
In 1972 they formed Papunya Tula Artists, owned by the artists.
Painters such as Clifford Possum Tjapaltjarri became internationally known.
Two great painters.
Albert Namatjira, a Western Arrernte man from Hermannsburg, Ntaria, learned watercolour in the 1930s and painted the MacDonnell Ranges in glowing colour.
He became a national celebrity, and in 1957 he and his wife Rubina were among the first Aboriginal people granted full citizenship rights.
Emily Kame Kngwarreye, an Anmatyerre woman from Utopia, began painting on canvas in her late 70s, around 1988.
In roughly eight years she produced thousands of works, from dense dots to sweeping lines.
She has since had major retrospectives in Canberra and London.
Her name is now often spelt Kngwarray.
Respect and ownership.
In Aboriginal law, the right to paint a story or design is usually inherited and held by specific people, with responsibilities to Country and kin.
Using designs without permission can be a serious breach.
Courts have recognised this, as in the 1994 'carpets case' over imported rugs copying artists' designs, and fake 'Aboriginal-style' souvenirs have led to penalties.
Namatjira's family lost control of his copyright after his death and regained it only in 2017.
When buying, look for Aboriginal-owned community art centres or dealers who sign the Indigenous Art Code.
Name the specific nation, such as Warlpiri or Yolŋu, rather than lumping everyone together.
Avoid 'primitive': this is a living, contemporary practice.
Some communities avoid images or names of people who have died, so heed warnings.
Let artists explain their work in their own words.
The key idea: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander art is many traditions, reflecting 250 or more distinct languages and peoples.
Part four. Michelangelo and the Sistine Chapel ceiling.
A sculptor who didn't want the job spent four years painting a chapel ceiling twenty metres above the floor.
He didn't do it lying on his back, either.
A reluctant painter.
In 1508, Michelangelo Buonarroti was in his early thirties and already famous for his marble David in Florence and his Pietà in Rome.
He thought of himself first as a sculptor.
Pope Julius II, a forceful and warlike pope, had hired him to carve a grand tomb, but then turned to decorating the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel, built by his uncle, Pope Sixtus IV.
Michelangelo had little experience of fresco and accepted reluctantly.
The walls already held frescoes by leading painters such as Botticelli and Perugino.
The ceiling, painted as a starry sky, was about to be transformed.
Painting on wet plaster.
Fresco means fresh in Italian.
The painter applies pigments mixed with water onto wet lime plaster.
As the plaster dries, a chemical reaction locks the colour into the wall, making it extremely durable.
The catch is speed.
Each day only as much plaster as could be painted before it set was laid.
These daily patches are called giornate, from the Italian for a day's work.
Mistakes could not be painted over; the plaster had to be chipped away and redone.
Michelangelo's team transferred his designs to the plaster using full-size drawings called cartoons, either by pricking holes along the lines or by pressing them into the soft surface.
Standing, not lying down.
A popular image shows Michelangelo lying on his back for years, paint dripping onto his face.
In reality, he designed a wooden scaffold that bridged the chapel just below the ceiling, leaving the floor free for services.
He and his assistants worked standing, heads tilted back and arms raised.
It was still punishing.
Michelangelo wrote a comic poem, with a little sketch in the margin, complaining about his aching neck, bent back and the paint dripping onto his face.
Nor did he work entirely alone, as another myth claims.
Assistants ground pigments, prepared plaster and helped with some painting, although he painted the great majority of the figures himself.
The story overhead.
The ceiling is about 40 metres long and 13 metres wide, with more than 300 figures.
Down the centre run nine scenes from Genesis, from God separating light from darkness to the story of Noah.
Around them sit huge prophets and sibyls, prophetesses from the classical world, and muscular nude youths called ignudi on painted architecture that only looks three-dimensional.
Michelangelo painted the scenes in reverse story order, starting near the entrance with Noah, and his figures grew larger as he went.
In The Creation of Adam, fingertips almost meet.
Some writers say the shape around God resembles a brain, hidden by Michelangelo the anatomist, but there is no evidence he intended it.
Judgment and restoration.
The ceiling was unveiled in 1512 and stunned everyone who saw it.
More than two decades later, Michelangelo painted The Last Judgment across the wall behind the altar, working from 1536 to 1541.
Christ raises the saved while the damned tumble towards hell.
Some church officials were scandalised by the nudity, and after his death Daniele da Volterra was hired to paint drapery over figures, earning the nickname Il Braghettone, the breeches maker.
For centuries, candle and incense smoke and old varnish darkened the ceiling.
A Vatican restoration from 1980 to 1994 revealed vivid pinks, greens, oranges and blues.
It was controversial, with some critics arguing that final touches were lost.
The chapel still hosts the conclave that elects a pope.
The key idea: Pope Julius II hired Michelangelo, who saw himself as a sculptor, to paint the Sistine Chapel ceiling in 1508.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What did very old cave art found in Indonesia overturn?
Answer. The idea that cave art began in Europe.
Question two. How can ochre be turned into paint?
Answer. By grinding it and mixing it with water or fat.
Question three. What does Arnhem Land's fine cross-hatching, called rarrk, help show?
Answer. Aboriginal art is many regional traditions.
Question four. How did Michelangelo see himself when he accepted the commission?
Answer. First of all as a sculptor, new to fresco.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
